summary: Updates RFC 2132 to reclassify DHCPv4 option codes 128 to 223 as publicly defined options managed by IANA under RFC 2939. IANA is directed to make these codes available for future assignment as public DHCP options.

eli5.summary: A block of seats once held for private use is now opened to the public, and a registrar will hand them out in an orderly way.

questions: what dhcp option codes were reclassified
how many site specific dhcp options remain
how did vendors claim reclassified dhcp options
why was dhcpv4 option space running out
subtitle: How DHCPv4 gained room for more public option codes by taking them from the little-used site-specific range.

tldr.problem: The publicly defined DHCPv4 option codes, 1 to 127, were nearly used up, while the site-specific range of 128 to 254 was large and little used for its intended purpose.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reclassifies option codes 128 to 223 as publicly defined, leaving 224 to 254 site-specific, and sets a staged IANA procedure that lets vendors already using a code claim it if they document it in time.
tldr.outcome: Codes 128 to 223 became available for future public assignment under RFC 2939, and RFC 3942 updates RFC 2132.

today: RFC 3942 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 2132.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A DHCPv4 message can carry options, each identified by a code. The publicly defined range, options 1 to 127, is nearly used up. Efforts such as RFC 3679 help extend its life, but the space will eventually run out.

RFC 3942 extends that public space by reclassifying much of the site-specific option range, which has not been widely used for its original purpose. It updates RFC 2132 and uses the key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY as defined in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: The public list of numbered slots was almost full. This note makes more slots by borrowing from a private list that was barely used.

sections.title: How the Option Space Was Divided
sections.content:
The option space runs from 0 to 255. Per RFC 2132, options 1 to 127 are publicly defined and are now allocated under RFC 2939, and options 128 to 254 are site-specific. Options 0 (pad) and 255 (end) are special and are defined in RFC 2131.

The site-specific range has 127 options. It was meant for configuration local to one site, and the RFC finds it hard to believe that a site needs that many. It also notes that many DHCP client implementations offer no well documented way to request site-specific options from a server or to let applications read the returned values.

Some vendors used site-specific codes to configure features of their products. That goes against the intent of the range, because such options are then specific to many sites. Trouble could follow if a site already used the same codes for something else, or if two vendors picked the same codes.
sections.eli5: The private section was meant for one building's own needs, but some companies used it for products sold everywhere. That could cause mix-ups when two uses picked the same number.

sections.title: The Alternatives the DHC Working Group Weighed
sections.content:
The DHC working group evaluated three ways to get a longer-term solution. Two were rejected.

  • 16-bit options in codes 126 and 127. Proposed by Ralph Droms in late 1996, but it penalizes the first option assigned to the new space, since it forces implementation of 16-bit option support. Options 126 and 127 were instead reclaimed by RFC 3679.
  • A new magic cookie and a 16-bit option code format. It also penalizes the first option, needs significant changes to clients, servers and relay agents, could hurt existing implementations that do not check the magic cookie value, requires both message formats to be supported for the foreseeable future, and makes clients send multiple DHCPDISCOVER messages, one per magic cookie.
  • Reclassifying part of the site-specific codes as public. The impact is minimal, as only sites presently using options in the reclassified range need to renumber them.

The third approach is the one this RFC adopts.
sections.eli5: They could have invented a whole new numbering system, which would have forced everyone to change. Moving a few slots from the private list to the public list bothered far fewer people, so they chose that.

sections.title: Reclassifying Options 128 to 223
sections.content:
Site-specific option codes 128 to 223 are reclassified as publicly defined, which leaves 31 site-specific options, 224 to 254. To let vendors that already use codes in that range publish their usage and request an official assignment, the RFC sets a staged procedure.

  1. IANA places codes 128 to 223 in the Unavailable state. They cannot yet be assigned as public options.
  2. Vendors using one or more of these codes have 6 months from the RFC's publication date to notify the DHC working group and IANA and agree to document the usage in an RFC. IANA then moves those codes to Tentatively Assigned. Vendors have 18 months to start documentation by submitting an Internet-Draft.
  3. Codes still Unavailable after 6 months move to Unassigned and may then be assigned as new public options under RFC 2939.
  4. For Tentatively Assigned codes, the documented usage MUST be consistent with the existing usage. When the usage is published as an RFC, IANA moves the code to Assigned. If no Internet-Draft is published within 18 months, or one expires after 18 months, IANA moves the code to Unassigned.

If several vendors of the same option number come forward and can show reasonably wide use, none of them may keep the current number. They MUST go through the normal process for a publicly assigned option under RFC 2939.

Sites presently using codes in the reclassified range SHOULD renumber those options to values within the remaining range. A site that needs more than 31 site-specific options must switch to suboptions, as has been done for other options such as the Relay Agent Information Option (RFC 3046).
sections.eli5: Everyone is told the numbers are on hold. Anyone who already uses one has six months to raise a hand, and then about a year and a half to write it down properly. Numbers nobody claims go back into the pool.

sections.title: IANA Actions and Security
sections.content:
The IANA section asks IANA to expand the publicly defined DHCPv4 option space from 1 to 127 up to 1 to 223. The new options, 128 to 223, are listed as Unavailable and MUST NOT be assigned to any publicly defined option at first. IANA is also asked to list claimed options as Tentatively Assigned, to make remaining Unavailable options available after 6 months, and to return Tentatively Assigned options to Unavailable after 18 months when no unexpired Internet-Draft documents the usage.

The wording of that section differs slightly from the main procedure: it says Available where Section 4 says Unassigned, and says a lapsed Tentatively Assigned code goes back to Unavailable. The intended flow is the same.

The security section is short. The document provides no security by itself and does not affect the existing DHCP security described in RFC 2131.
sections.eli5: The registrar is asked to update the official list to match, and nothing here makes DHCP more or less safe.
